front: Single vs double vs triple bonds?
back: More shared pairs → shorter and stronger bonds.

front: Octet rule and two common exceptions (SL)?
back: Atoms tend to reach 8 valence electrons by sharing. Incomplete octets: Be (4 e⁻, BeCl₂) and B (6 e⁻, BF₃).
Electron domains (bonding pairs, lone pairs, multiple bonds) around the central atom repel and arrange as far apart as possible; a double/triple bond counts as one domain.

front: Shapes of molecules with 3 domains (1 lone pair) and 4 domains (2 lone pairs)?
back: 3 domains, 1 LP: bent, <120° (~117°, SO₂). 4 domains, 2 LP: bent 104.5° (H₂O). 4 domains, 1 LP: trigonal pyramidal 107° (NH₃).
Lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bonding pair > bonding pair–bonding pair; each lone pair closes the bond angle by ~2.5°.

front: Why is CO₂ non-polar but H₂O polar?
back: Both have polar bonds. CO₂ is linear so the bond dipoles cancel; H₂O is bent so they do not.
Attractions between instantaneous and induced dipoles from electron movement; present between all molecules; increase with number of electrons (molar mass) and surface area.
Dipole–dipole: between permanent dipoles of polar molecules. Dipole–induced dipole: a polar molecule distorts the electron cloud of a neighbour.

front: Why is the boiling point of H₂O much higher than H₂S?
back: Water forms hydrogen bonds (O is highly electronegative and small); H₂S has only weaker dipole–dipole and London forces.

front: Does boiling a molecular substance break covalent bonds?
back: No. Boiling overcomes intermolecular forces only; the covalent bonds within molecules stay intact.

front: Why is ethanol miscible with water but hexane isn’t?
back: "Like dissolves like": ethanol forms hydrogen bonds with water; non-polar hexane cannot, so water–water H-bonds are not replaced.
Diamond: each C sp³, 4 covalent bonds, tetrahedral, rigid. Graphite: each C sp², 3 bonds in hexagonal layers, delocalised electrons, London forces between layers.

front: Why does graphite conduct electricity but diamond does not?
back: In graphite each C has one delocalised electron free to move along the layers; in diamond all four valence electrons are in localised bonds.
Molecular sphere of 60 sp² C in pentagons and hexagons; London forces between molecules so low mp, poor conductor; soluble in non-polar solvents.
Giant covalent lattice: each Si bonded tetrahedrally to 4 O, each O to 2 Si — very high mp, hard, non-conductor.

front: Why do components separate in chromatography?
back: Different relative affinities for the stationary and mobile phases (polarity/solubility); components with greater affinity for the mobile phase move further (higher Rf).
All six C–C bonds are the same length (between single and double); enthalpy of hydrogenation is less exothermic than predicted for three C=C; prefers substitution to addition.
Two resonance structures; bent (~117°), central O sp² with a lone pair; both O–O bonds equal, bond order 1.5; polar.

front: (HL) Bond order in a resonance hybrid (e.g. CO₃²⁻)?
back: Total bonding pairs between the atoms ÷ number of positions: 4 ÷ 3 = 1.33 for each C–O in carbonate.

front: (HL) Shapes of XeF₄, SF₄ and ClF₃?
back: XeF₄: square planar 90° (6 domains, 2 LP). SF₄: seesaw (5 domains, 1 LP). ClF₃: T-shaped (5 domains, 2 LP).

front: (HL) Why is a π bond weaker and more reactive than a σ bond?
back: Sideways overlap is less effective; π electron density lies above and below the bond axis, exposed to electrophiles. Also prevents rotation about C=C.

front: (HL) Hybridisation of C in ethane, ethene, ethyne?
back: Ethane sp³ (109.5°); ethene sp² (120°, one unhybridised p forms π); ethyne sp (180°, two p orbitals form two π).
